title: NorthLight Analytics - Surge & Concurrency: hosting decision
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets for streaming responses, burst concurrency planning, and whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployment better fits NorthLight's SLA and security constraints. Discussed KV/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, and a small benchmarking plan (token/sec + p95) for next week.
topics: p95 targets for chat streaming (target 300-500ms for short responses)
burst concurrency and warm pool sizing
hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
benchmarking plan: tokens/sec, p95, cold vs warm starts
action_items: Jordan Blake: Share hosted vs dedicated pricing spreadsheet and sample SLA (due 2027-08-06)
Leila Chen: Draft benchmark harness steps + sample load script (k6 + custom token feeder) and share repo link (due 2027-08-09)
Marcus Hale: Provide realistic traffic traces (1 week) and target p95 SLOs (due 2027-08-07)
Elena Ortiz: Confirm model families + average prompt/response token lengths (due 2027-08-06)
next_steps: Run a 3-day token/sec + p95 pilot on Redwood Hosted using customer's sample traces
If pilot shows warmup/cold start risk, scope Dedicated reserved pool sizing
Redwood to share security pack (SOC2, ISO docs) and private deployment checklist
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-04
Time: 15:30 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recording: yes

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood. With me is Leila, our solutions engineer. Quick agenda: understand your p95 targets, concurrency patterns, and any security constraints so we can recommend Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

[00:22] Priya Raman: Thanks Jordan. High level: we're building a real-time analytics assistant for ops teams. For short lookups we need p95 around 350ms ideally, but for longer multi-turn conversations we can tolerate 800-1,200ms. Big question is how to architect for bursty traffic — our peak is pretty spiky.

[00:45] Leila Chen: Got it. Can you quantify "spiky" — concurrent streams, tokens per second?

[00:52] Marcus Hale: Yeah, our current estimate is baseline 30 concurrent streams, with spikes up to 600 concurrent for 2-6 minute windows triggered by dashboards refresh. Typical short query is 40-80 tokens total, longer flows 400-1,200 tokens.

[01:12] Jordan Blake: Useful, thanks. And what are hard constraints — is data residency or VPC required?

[01:20] Priya Raman: We need VPC peering for the private deployment option because some telemetry contains customer identifiers. SOC2 is a must, and KMS integration for key management. We prefer not to send PII to a multi-tenant vendor unless masked.

[01:36] Leila Chen: That maps to our common patterns. Hosted gives fastest time-to-value; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives the most control for KMS and network. Tradeoffs: cost and ops complexity go up as you move from Hosted -> Dedicated -> Private.

[02:02] Elena Ortiz: From ML side, we care about quantization options and how that impacts accuracy. Also KV cache/prefix caching is interesting — many queries will share prefixes. Can Redwood do prefix caching across requests to reduce token compute?

[02:20] Leila Chen: Yes, our runtime supports prefix/KV cache caching for model families that expose KV cache. That reduces repeated computation for multi-turn and for common prefixes. It also plays nicely with batching. Note: caching effectiveness depends on the degree of prefix reuse. We'll want to look at traces to estimate hit rates.

[02:44] Marcus Hale: On batching — we can't do big batch windows because we need low latency for interactive queries. Hoping batching won't add more than 50-100ms on average.

[03:01] Leila Chen: Continuous batching optimizes for latency-sensitive workloads — it tries small micro-batches that keep latency down while improving GPU utilization. You can tune max batch window and target latency SLO. For Hosted we manage that; for Dedicated you can also provide custom policies.

[03:24] Priya Raman: How about cold-start behavior — when a spike shows up and instances need to spin up, what are warm pool and burst options?

[03:34] Jordan Blake: Good question. Our Dedicated offering supports a warm pool and burst capacity. You can reserve base capacity and allow short bursts to a higher tier. For Hosted we have regional fallback and prewarmed replicas for customers on higher tiers. Cold starts depend on model size — small LLaMA-like variants spin up faster than large 70B families.

[03:58] Elena Ortiz: We plan to use a 7B-ish family for most queries and 34-70B for some complex scoring. Need to understand p95 impact across those models.

[04:10] Leila Chen: As you move up in model size, the per-token latency and memory footprint rises. For streaming p95, shorter responses (40-80 tokens) are dominated by initial attention costs and context handling. For 7B we typically see sub-200ms per-token generation on A100-like hardware for small sequences under ideal batching; 34/70B are higher. But important caveat: those numbers vary with quantization, kernels, and whether KV cache is hot.

[04:42] Marcus Hale: Can you run a token/sec benchmark? We want to measure steady-state tokens/sec and p95 for streaming so we can size GPUs and warm pool.

[04:51] Jordan Blake: Absolutely — typical pilot is: you provide traces, we run a hosted pilot with realistic traffic, capture p95 (streaming interleaved) and tokens/sec. If the pilot shows we can hit your SLOs with Hosted we recommend starting there; otherwise we size Dedicated.

[05:08] Priya Raman: What's the expected turnaround for that pilot?

[05:12] Leila Chen: We can stand up a 3-day pilot within 48-72 hours of getting traces and a quick onboarding token. The benchmark harness will record p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cold vs warm starts, and cost per 1M tokens. We'll share raw logs and a spreadsheet with results.

[05:32] Samir Qureshi: Any specific instrument or tool you use for load? We run k6 internally but can adapt.

[05:37] Leila Chen: k6 is fine; we normally use a small driver plus a token feeder to replay real traces. We also have a lightweight harness we can share — link to repo in the follow-up.

[05:48] Priya Raman: On security again — for Hosted, what's the isolation model? Are there dedicated tenancy options?

[05:56] Jordan Blake: Hosted is multi-tenant but SOC2 compliant and we support customer-managed encryption keys (bring-your-own-key) in some enterprise tiers. If isolation is required, Dedicated provides tenant isolation via reserved capacity and VPC peering options. Private deployments are fully customer-controlled.

[06:14] Marcus Hale: I want to call out an important constraint: our infra team cannot accept external sidecars running in our VPC; any private deployment needs to be a managed package we can run inside a restricted subnet.

[06:27] Leila Chen: Noted. We have an on-prem package that runs in air-gapped or restricted subnets; we'll include the deployment checklist.

[06:35] Jordan Blake: Let's go through an example sizing exercise quickly. If you target p95 350ms for short queries at 600 concurrent spikes, assume 50 tokens/request average. That means roughly X tokens/sec — okay I'll do math out loud. 600 concurrent * (1 req per 0.5s) ~ 1,200 req/s, * 50 tokens = 60k tokens/sec peak. Does that sound in the ballpark?

[07:01] Marcus Hale: Our spikes are bursts of dashboard reloads — closer to 1,000-1,500 req/s for 30 seconds in extreme events, so numbers could be higher.

[07:11] Jordan Blake: Right — so in worst-case we should plan for 75k-100k tokens/sec bursts. For steady-state the number's much lower. Key levers: batching and KV cache can reduce compute per request; quantization reduces per-token latency and memory enabling higher tokens/sec per GPU.

[07:32] Elena Ortiz: On quantization — how aggressive can you be without hurting downstream extraction quality? We have a small NLU model that fails on aggressive 4-bit quantization sometimes.

[07:42] Leila Chen: We'll recommend specific quantization profiles per model family and validate on your eval prompts. Redwood Optimize also runs quality regressions so you can see if 4-bit affects your metrics. Often 4-bit works on decoder-only models with minimal delta, but we'll validate.

[07:58] Priya Raman: If we push to Dedicated, how much ops overhead is expected on our side?

[08:03] Jordan Blake: Dedicated is managed by Redwood with reserved GPU pools. You get an assigned infra contact. You do need to provide VPC peering and some network config; we can handle autoscaling policies and prewarm rules, but you own some elements of monitoring integration. If you want zero ops, Private is heavier but gives you full control.

[08:22] Samir Qureshi: For the pilot, should we mask PII in traces or can we share as-is?

[08:28] Jordan Blake: For Hosted pilot, we prefer masked traces. For Dedicated pilots we can also accept traces behind a signed NDA and short-lived keys. We'll follow whatever your security team requires.

[08:39] Marcus Hale: Cost sensitivity: if we move Dedicated, what's the delta vs Hosted? Ballpark numbers are fine.

[08:46] Jordan Blake: Ballpark: Hosted is pay-as-you-go with some enterprise tiers; for heavy steady-state Dedicated often reduces unit cost due to reserved capacity. We'll share a detailed pricing spreadsheet but expect Dedicated to be higher fixed cost but lower incremental per-token.

[09:02] Leila Chen: Also consider multi-region routing: if your customers are global, we can route by latency and failover to another region/model variant to meet p95 during partial outages.

[09:15] Priya Raman: We also care about model fallbacks — if a 70B path is too slow during a spike, can we automatically fallback to a 7B variant?

[09:22] Leila Chen: Yes, Redwood has routing policies to do model variant fallbacks by latency or cost thresholds. You can set canary/rollout rules and automatic fallback to compatible variants when capacity is constrained.

[09:35] Jordan Blake: Ok quick pause — do you all have any blockers that would prevent a 3-day pilot?

[09:41] Priya Raman: No blockers from leadership; we need Marcus to confirm traces and Elena the model list. Security will need the SOC2 docs, but that's standard.

[09:52] Marcus Hale: I'll pull traces; need to scrub PII for Hosted.

[10:00] Samir Qureshi: Timeline question — if pilot looks promising and we go Dedicated, how long to provision reserved pool?

[10:07] Jordan Blake: Dedicated provisioning typically takes 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region. We can do an interim approach of Hosted with prewarmed replicas while Dedicated is stood up.

[10:18] Leila Chen: Let's talk specifics of the benchmark we'll run: we capture streaming p95 at the token chunk level, tokens/sec steady-state, end-to-end client-observed latency, cold vs warm start delta, and GPU util. We'll also annotate whether KV cache hits occurred and share a cost estimate normalized per 1M tokens.

[10:41] Elena Ortiz: Good — also include a 90-minute stress run to emulate the dashboard storm. We want to see how graceful degradation looks and fallback latency.

[10:50] Leila Chen: We'll include that.

[11:00] Priya Raman: One more — SSO/SAML integration?

[11:05] Jordan Blake: Supported for enterprise tiers; we'll add integration docs.

[11:10] Priya Raman: Anything else on observability? We want token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency traces.

[11:16] Leila Chen: Redwood Console provides per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, and tracing hooks. We'll demo that in the follow-up if useful.

[11:27] Marcus Hale: Can you share an example dashboard export?

[11:30] Jordan Blake: Yes — I'll attach a sample export and a benchmark spreadsheet after the call.

[11:40] Priya Raman: Ok last thing — if we need private deployment, is there a minimal hardware footprint you recommend for our 7B/34B mix?

[11:48] Leila Chen: Roughly for 7B you can target 1-2 A100s per steady-state shard depending on quantization; 34B needs multiple GPUs or 80GB+ variants. We'll produce a sizing matrix after we see traces.

[12:05] Jordan Blake: Great. Quick recap: Jordan will send pricing spreadsheet and security pack; Leila will share benchmark harness and run pilot once traces are provided; Marcus and Elena to provide traces and model list. Next checkpoint: review pilot results and decide Hosted vs Dedicated within two weeks.

[12:28] Priya Raman: Sounds good, thanks all.

[12:33] Jordan Blake: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with links: deck (LINK: https://redwood.example/deck/nla-hosting-decision), benchmark repo (LINK: https://github.com/redwoodinc/bench-harness), and pricing spreadsheet (LINK: https://redwood.example/pricing/nla-preview).

[12:50] End of recording.

Notes: Transcript contains a few microphone cuts and occasional speaker overlap. Some technical terms may be auto-transcribed incorrectly (e.g., model family names).
